artworks.title: Hypnos and Thanatos Carry Sarpedon (Euphronios Krater)
artworks.description: Euphronios' calyx-krater — Sleep and Death lifting Zeus' Lycian son from the Trojan plain under Hermes' eye — remains the definitive image of Sarpedon's fall.

artworks.title: The Dead Sarpedon, Borne by Sleep and Death
artworks.description: Scott's National Galleries of Scotland canvas from the Iliad: Hypnos and Thanatos bear the fallen Lycian prince — Romantic pathos for Zeus' son whom even a father could not save.

artworks.title: Sleep and Death Conveying the Body of Sarpedon to Lycia
artworks.description: A nineteenth-century illustration of the Homeric cortege: Sleep and Death carry Sarpedon home to Lycia — the Iliad's most solemn funeral flight.

artworks.title: Death of Sarpedon (bell-krater)
artworks.description: Attic red-figure bell-krater of the Sarpedon type: winged Sleep and Death lift the hero's body — the Euphronios theme repeated for another symposium.

artworks.title: Death of Sarpedon
artworks.description: Lucanian red-figure hydria in the Museo Nazionale della Siritide, Policoro: Sarpedon's corpse amid Amazons and attendants — South Italian vase-painting keeping the Lycian prince's death in circulation.

popCulture.title: Iliad
popCulture.creator: Homer
popCulture.description: Books XII and XVI — the rain of blood, Patroclus' spear, and Zeus deciding not to save his own son.

popCulture.title: Euphronios Krater
popCulture.description: The Sarpedon krater — once Met, now Cerveteri — made the Lycian hero modern archaeology's most famous corpse.

popCulture.title: Sarpedon
popCulture.description: Zeus' mortal son who dies at Troy — the Iliad's lesson that even a god's child is not exempt from fate.
